'''Jason David Williams''' (born September 10, 1981) is an American former [[basketball]] player and television analyst. He played [[college basketball]] for the [[Duke Blue Devils men's basketball|Duke Blue Devils]] and professionally for the [[Chicago Bulls]] in the [[National Basketball Association]] (NBA).

Then known as Jason Williams, he won the [[2001 NCAA Men's Division I Basketball Tournament|2001 NCAA Championship]] with Duke, and was named [[NABC Player of the Year]] in 2001 and 2002. He was drafted second overall in the [[2002 NBA draft]] by the Bulls. He was known as Jay on joining the Bulls to avoid confusion with two other players with similar names in the NBA at the time.<ref>[[Jason Williams (basketball, born 1975)|Jason Williams]] and [[Jayson Williams]]</ref> His playing career was effectively ended by a motorcycle crash in 2003. He last played with the [[Austin Toros]] of the [[NBA Development League]] in 2006 when his season was ended early due to lingering physical effects from his accident.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.nba.com/dleague/news/Bell_Williams_061230.html |title=The Official Site Of The Nba Development League: Austin Toros |work=Nba.com |access-date=March 29, 2010 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090115094645/http://www.nba.com/dleague/news/Bell_Williams_061230.html |archive-date=January 15, 2009 }}</ref>

Since retiring, Williams has worked as an analyst for [[ESPN]]. Initially working on ''[[ESPN College Basketball]]'', he was reassigned to the NBA full-time with his addition on ESPN's ''[[NBA Countdown]]'' program in 2019.

==High school==
Williams grew up in [[Plainfield, New Jersey]], and attended [[St. Joseph High School (Metuchen, New Jersey)|St. Joseph High School]] in [[Metuchen, New Jersey|Metuchen]], graduating in 1999. He not only excelled at basketball, but took an active interest in other activities, most notably [[chess]]. His nickname in high school was "Jay Dubs". Williams also played junior varsity soccer during his freshman year and was the state volleyball player of the year during his senior year. In basketball that year, Williams was named a First Team All-State Player in New Jersey, the New Jersey Player of the Year, a ''Parade'' All-American, a ''USA Today'' first team All-American, and a [[McDonald's All-American]], where he competed in the Slam Dunk Contest and the McDonald's All-American Game, scoring 20 points in the contest. In his last year of high school he averaged 19 points, 7.0 assists, 4.2 rebounds and 3.7 steals per game; he had started each of the 4 years he spent at St. Joseph, and set school records in total points (1,977) and steals (407).<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.usatoday.com/sports/preps/basketba/99allusab.htm|title=Harvey named national player of the year|access-date=April 13, 2012|date=May 21, 1999|work=[[USA Today]]}}</ref> He was also named the recipient of the 1999 Morgan Wootten Award for his basketball achievements and his work in the classroom, where he maintained a 3.6 GPA.

==College career==
At [[Duke University]], Williams, a {{convert|6|ft|2|in|adj=on}}, {{convert|195|lb|adj=on}} [[point guard]], became one of the few freshmen in school history to average double figures in scoring and was named ACC Rookie of the Year and National Freshman of the Year by The Sporting News, averaging 15.5 points, 6.5 assists and 4.2 rebounds per contest. He was also a first team Freshman All-American by ''[[Basketball Times]]''.{{citation needed|date=August 2018}}

The next season Williams started all 39 games and led the Devils to the 2001 NCAA National Championship, earning NABC Player of the Year honors. His 841 points broke [[Dick Groat]]'s 49-year Duke record for points in a season, while he led all tournament scorers with a 25.7 points per game average. Williams also set the NCAA Tournament record for three-pointers attempted (66), while also making 132 three-point field goals—good for the sixth-highest total in NCAA history. His 21.6 points per game led the ACC and made him the first Duke player since Danny Ferry (1989) to lead the league in scoring. His 6.1 assists were good for second in the league, while he also ranked second in three-point field goal percentage (.427) and first in three-pointers made (3.4 per game). Williams was widely considered the best player in college basketball, earning both the prestigious [[Naismith College Player of the Year|Naismith Award]] and [[Wooden Award]] as College Basketball's Player of the Year in 2002. He graduated with a degree in sociology in 2002, and left Duke with 2,079 points, good for sixth all-time, and with his [[jersey number]] 22 [[Jersey retirement#Retired numbers|retired]] at Senior Day.

He had 36 double-figure scoring games in a single season (tied for 5th-most in Duke history as of March 28, 2010, with [[Jon Scheyer]], [[Shane Battier]], and [[JJ Redick]]).<ref name="goduke1">{{cite web |url=http://www.goduke.com/ViewArticle.dbml?SPSID=22724&SPID=1845&DB_OEM_ID=4200&ATCLID=204918040 |title=Notes: Duke 78, Baylor 71 – Duke University Blue Devils | Official Athletics Site |date=March 28, 2010 |publisher=GoDuke.com |access-date=March 29, 2010 |archive-date=December 5, 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141205091943/http://www.goduke.com/ViewArticle.dbml?SPSID=22724&SPID=1845&DB_OEM_ID=4200&ATCLID=204918040 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

In 2001–02, Williams, [[Carlos Boozer]], and [[Mike Dunleavy Jr.]] each scored at least 600 points for the season, a feat only matched at Duke by Jon Scheyer, [[Kyle Singler]], and [[Nolan Smith]] in the 2009–10 season.<ref name="goduke1" /> Williams (841) and [[Shane Battier]] (778) on the 2001 national championship team were one of only two Duke duos to each score over 700 points in a season, the other duo being Scheyer (728) and Singler (707) in the 2009–10 season.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.goduke.com/ViewArticle.dbml?SPSID=22724&SPID=1845&DB_OEM_ID=4200&ATCLID=204923002 |title=Notes: Duke 61, Butler 59 – Duke University Blue Devils | Official Athletics Site |publisher=GoDuke.com |date=December 5, 2009 |access-date=April 6, 2010 |archive-date=February 1, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190201013745/http://www.goduke.com/ViewArticle.dbml?SPSID=22724&SPID=1845&DB_OEM_ID=4200&ATCLID=204923002 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

==Professional career==

=== Chicago Bulls (2002–2004) ===
Williams was selected by the [[Chicago Bulls]] with the second overall pick in the [[2002 NBA draft]], after [[Yao Ming]] was selected by the [[Houston Rockets]]. Williams was a starter in the Bulls' line-up for most of the [[2002–03 NBA season]]. Although his performance was inconsistent and he competed for playing time with [[Jamal Crawford]], he showed signs of promise, including posting a [[triple-double]] in a win over the [[New Jersey Nets]]. Williams' final NBA game was played on April 15, 2003, in a 115–106 win over the [[Philadelphia 76ers]] in which he recorded 15 points, 7 assists, 2 rebounds, and 1 steal.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Jay Williams 2002-03 Stats per Game - NBA |url=https://www.espn.com/nba/player/gamelog/_/id/1733/jay-williams |access-date=2024-02-19 |website=ESPN |language=en}}</ref>

====Motorcycle accident====
On the night of June 19, 2003, Williams was riding a motorcycle at a fast speed on the North Side of [[Chicago]]. He crashed his [[Yamaha YZF-R6]] motorcycle into a streetlight at the intersection of Honore Street and Fletcher Street near the [[North Center, Chicago#Roscoe Village|Roscoe Village]] neighborhood. Williams was not wearing a helmet, nor was he licensed to ride a motorcycle in [[Illinois]], and he was also violating the terms of his NBA Bulls contract by riding a motorcycle.<ref>{{cite web|author=Ian Thomsen |url=http://vault.sportsillustrated.cnn.com/vault/article/magazine/MAG1029108/index.htm |archive-url=https://archive.today/20120722010910/http://vault.sportsillustrated.cnn.com/vault/article/magazine/MAG1029108/index.htm |url-status=dead |archive-date=July 22, 2012 |title=After Jay Williams's motorcycle crash, the Bulls' new G.M. – 07.07.03 – SI Vault |publisher=[[Sports Illustrated]] |date=July 7, 2003 |access-date=March 29, 2010 }}</ref> Williams' injuries included a fractured [[human pelvis|pelvis]], a severed main nerve in his leg, and three torn ligaments in his left [[knee]], including the [[Anterior cruciate ligament injury|ACL]]. He required lengthy [[physical therapy]] to regain the use of his leg. A week after the motorcycle crash, the Bulls drafted point guard [[Kirk Hinrich]]. When it became clear Williams would not be returning to the Bulls for a long time, if at all, because of his severe injuries, the Bulls chose to waive him and drop him from the roster. This left the team without their top draft pick from just a year prior. Legally, the Bulls did not have to pay Williams any remaining salary at all because his severe injuries occurred while he violated the terms of his contract by riding a motorcycle; however, the Bulls organization decided to give Williams $3 million when they waived him so Williams could use the funds toward his rehabilitation expenses. Williams apologized to the Bulls organization for violating the terms of his contract and severely injuring himself. He stated at the time that he would work hard in his physical rehabilitation so that he could make a return to the Bulls. In his 2016 memoir, he mentioned that he became addicted to illegal painkillers as well as other drugs after the accident.<ref>Life is not an Accident, William Jay, p. 258-9</ref>

===Austin Toros (2006)===
On September 28, 2006, the [[New Jersey Nets]] announced that they had signed Williams to a non-guaranteed contract. However, on October 22, the Nets released him.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.espn.com/nba/news/story?id=2635166 |title=ESPN – Jay Williams, in comeback attempt, cut by Nets – NBA |publisher=[[ESPN]] |date=October 23, 2006 |access-date=March 29, 2010}}</ref>

Williams then signed with the [[Austin Toros]] of the [[NBA Development League]], but he played in just three games for the club. On December 30, 2006, the Toros waived him due to injury.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nba.com/dleague/dleague/transactions.html |title=NBA Development League: Transactions Index |work=Nba.com |date=November 27, 2009 |access-date=March 29, 2010 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111101144313/http://www.nba.com/dleague/dleague/transactions.html |archive-date=November 1, 2011 }}</ref> Williams subsequently announced that he had no plans to resume his basketball career.

==National team career==
During his basketball playing career, Williams also represented the senior [[United States men's national basketball team|USA national basketball team]]. He was a part of the US team that finished in 6th place at the [[2002 FIBA World Cup]], which was held in [[Indianapolis]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.usab.com/history/national-team-mens/fourteenth-world-championship-2002.aspx|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150429164327/http://www.usab.com/history/national-team-mens/fourteenth-world-championship-2002.aspx|url-status=dead|archive-date=April 29, 2015|title=FOURTEENTH WORLD CHAMPIONSHIP -- 2002|website=USAB.com|language=en|access-date=2021-02-24}}</ref> In seven games played during the tournament, Williams averaged 3.9 points, 1.0 rebounds, 1.6 assists, and 0.9 steals, in 6.6 minutes per game.<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20120731233624/http://archive.fiba.com/pages/eng/fa/player/p/pid/39179/sid/3118/tid/379/tid2/_/2002_World_Championship_for_Men/index.html 2002 World Championship for Men USA 12 - Jason Williams.]</ref>

==Post-basketball career==
[[File:Jay Williams ESPN.jpg|thumb|Williams on [[ESPN]] in January 2011]]
Williams works for [[ESPN]] as an NBA analyst. Previously, Williams covered college basketball for the network.<ref>ESPN MediaZone (2010). Williams is widely known for being the Spokesperson of Visions Federal Credit Union, headquartered in Endwell, New York. [http://www.espnmediazone3.com/us/2010/05/12/williams_jay/ Jay Williams] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120616045037/http://www.espnmediazone3.com/us/2010/05/12/williams_jay/ |date=June 16, 2012 }}. Accessed June 23, 2012.</ref> He has also done motivational speaking and worked as an analyst on [[CBS College Sports Network]] during the [[2008 NCAA men's basketball tournament]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.dailyherald.com/story/?id=72421&src=150 |title='Active' Noah's NBA debut a rare bright spot |publisher=Daily Herald |access-date=March 29, 2010}}</ref> He was a recruiter for sports agency Ceruzzi Sports and Entertainment from 2007 to 2009.<ref>Rivals.com (2009). [https://sports.yahoo.com/ncaa/basketball/news?slug=ys-agents031109 Agents and AAU: Unrequited Love]. Accessed June 23, 2012.</ref> In 2016, Williams released his autobiography, ''Life Is Not an Accident: A Memoir of Reinvention''.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Williams|first1=Jay|title=Life Is Not an Accident: A Memoir of Reinvention|date=January 26, 2016|publisher=Harper|isbn=978-0062327987|pages=272|url=https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/0062327984|access-date=February 2, 2016}}</ref> Presently, Williams is the Spokesperson of Visions Federal Credit Union, headquartered in Endwell, New York.<ref>{{cite AV media | date=October 16, 2015 | url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KdReOJ5KOi4 | title=Visions Introduces ESPN's Jay Williams as Spokesperson | via=YouTube }}</ref> He was also an announcer in [[NBA Live 19]].

According to a May 2020 article on BlackEnterprise.com, Williams co-founded a management consulting company named Simatree, serves as a partial owner of The CabinNYC restaurant, works as an advisor to a digital marketing agency, and partners with EPIC Insurance to provide financial guidance to athletes and celebrities.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Gumbs |first1=Alisa |title=blackenterprise.com |url=https://www.blackenterprise.com/espns-jay-williams-is-building-a-business-empire-behind-the-scenes/ |website=blackenterprise.com |date=May 22, 2020 |publisher=Black Enterprise |access-date=22 May 2020}}</ref>

In 2021, Williams began hosting a podcast series titled ''The Limits with Jay Williams'' for [[NPR]].<ref>{{cite press release |last1=Donovan |first1=Dave |title=NPR Announces New Podcast with Jay Williams |url=https://www.npr.org/about-npr/1035165597/npr-announces-new-podcast-with-jay-williams |access-date=15 October 2022 |work=[[NPR]] |date=9 September 2021 |language=en}}</ref>

Williams co-hosted the "Keyshawn, JWill & Max Show" national morning show on [[ESPN Radio]], with [[Keyshawn Johnson]] and [[Max Kellerman]].<ref>[https://www.insideradio.com/free/espn-new-york-98-7-expands-local-morning-show-drops-keyshawn-jwill-max/article_100c5ce4-7192-11ed-90dc-fbb839853948.html "'ESPN New York 98.7' Expands Local Morning Show; Drops 'Keyshawn, JWill & Max,'"] ''Insideradio.com'', December 1, 2022, retrieved March 7, 2023.</ref> In June 2023, it was canceled by ESPN as a part of their budget cuts.

==Personal life==
Williams is a cousin of former [[National Football League|NFL]] [[wide receiver]] [[David Tyree]].<ref>{{cite news |title=Jay Williams Can't Wait To Have More Space To Build Bridges On ESPN Radio |author=GoneTrending |date=August 17, 2020 |url=https://www.gonetrending.com/2020/08/17/jay-williams-interview-espn-radio-keyshawn-jwill-zubin/ |access-date=March 22, 2022}}</ref>

He is married to Nikki Bonacorsi and is the father of one daughter and one son.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://people.com/parents/jay-williams-daughter-amelia-serendipitous-life-fatherhood-exclusive/|title=Jay Williams Talks 'Serendipitous' Life as a Working Dad After Almost Dying in an Accident at 21|website=PEOPLE.com|language=en|access-date=2020-02-04}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://twitter.com/realjaywilliams/status/1380572594814906372|title=Jay Williams Announces the Birth of Another Child|website=twitter.com|language=en|access-date=2020-04-10}}</ref>
